my_independent_answer: Phasing in is not a zone change (permanent was never treated as having left/entered the battlefield); ETB triggers don't fire.
Deathtouch redefines lethal damage as any nonzero amount, so a trampling deathtouch creature need only assign 1 to each blocker before excess goes through.
Storm is a triggered ability on the stack; only ability-specific counters (e.g. Stifle) can counter it, not spell-only counters.
A hybrid symbol makes the card all listed colors for every purpose including color identity, so both colors must be in the commander's identity.
No player gets priority in the untap step, so nothing can be cast/activated; triggers wait until the next priority window (usually upkeep).
Creatures/battles/planeswalkers stay attacking/blocking for the whole end of combat step; removed from combat only as the step ends.
No, playing a land is a special action that never uses the stack and is never a spell, so it is not 'cast'.
answer_note: Answer correctly identifies and corrects the premise.
question_note: The question's own verb ('cast') presupposes lands are cast; 305.1 establishes playing a land is a special action, never a spell, so it is never cast. The gold answer handles this correctly (leads with 'No' and explains why), so the answer itself is fine, but the question as phrased embeds a false premise about the correct terminology for the action.

my_independent_answer: Yes. The evoke trigger doesn't target, it just says 'sacrifice it' referring to that specific permanent object. Per 400.7/403.4, once that permanent has left the battlefield (via any means) it becomes a new object with no relation to the one being referred to; per 701.21a you can't sacrifice something that isn't a permanent (on the battlefield, under your control); per 101.3, any part of an instruction that's impossible to perform is simply ignored. So the ability still resolves (no target to check-fail on) but the sacrifice clause does nothing.
answer_note: Substance is correct and matches my independent derivation. The drafter's flagged uncertainty is resolvable: rule 101.3 ('Any part of an instruction that's impossible to perform is ignored... if it doesn't [specify consequences], there's no effect') is the general rule that plugs the gap they were missing -- it's the direct answer to 'why does this silently fail rather than doing something else.' Citing 400.7/403.4 (object becomes new object on zone change) alongside 701.21a and 101.3 would make this airtight. Recommend adding 101.3 (and optionally 400.7) to cited_rules before this goes into the gold set, but the answer as written is not wrong.
question_note: Unambiguous single correct answer once the interaction rules are traced through; appropriately advanced (not trivial) -- a system relying on surface pattern-matching over targeting rules alone could plausibly get this wrong.
uncertainty_note: Same gap the drafter noted: no single CR rule says in evoke-specific terms 'if the permanent already left, this clause fizzles' -- the conclusion is correctly assembled from 701.21a + 101.3 (general instruction-impossibility rule) + 400.7 (new-object-on-zone-change), which is a solid combination but not one bespoke citation.

my_independent_answer: Yes, keyword abilities are abilities (just shorthand for rules text), so 'loses all abilities' strips them too.
question_note: Not trivial -- plausible failure mode for a system to treat keywords as a separate category from 'abilities'.

my_independent_answer: Yes, no rule caps hand size during the turn; enforcement is only at cleanup (discard down to max, normally 7).
It's put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action (no stack, checked whenever a player would get priority); can't actually go below 0 since loyalty is counters.
answer_note: The added note about not being able to go below 0 is correct and non-contradictory (loyalty is a counter count, floor is 0), doesn't change the outcome.
